storylines.title: The Crown
storylines.about: Told by the King in Rome. The Free Assembly rises against Church and Crown: Virginia in 2767, then the cities of the Crown.

still.caption: The King's study in Rome, by candlelight: the war map on the desk, the dome of Saint Peter's in the window.

lines: Sit by me. Move the candle, so you can see the map. That is the world as it was when I was young.
It begins in Virginia, on a tobacco plantation, in the summer of sixty-seven.
Fairleigh finished it in one morning, with canister. We drank to him in this room and called it over.
Now look at the map again, and put your finger on Nuremberg.
Hollweg built a clock that would not stop, and in one Advent night it took Nuremberg from him. He believed it could think.
He has rooms in the east wing now. He writes to me every week, long letters in a small hand, and I read them all.
Lindqvist's station on the Rio Negro burned on Saint John's Eve. To hear him tell it, he was robbed.
He is held in the palace now. No man living knows those animals better, so I listen to him, and I have what he says checked.
Lyon went home without a volley fired. Tomasz will tell you it was luck. It was Tomasz.
The printer gave us one word, Paris. We were slow to hear it.
I sent Varenne to sea. Tomasz asked for his life on his knees, and Fairleigh told me an exile does less harm than a martyr.
We shall see what he does with the years I gave him.
Varenne died on the Grève. I signed the sentence myself, and Tomasz sat with him the last night.
Within a month they were singing about him in every town in France.
Father Ferrer's report reached me before the first snow. Machines that pull out their own stop-works.
Hollweg kept the broken ones to study. I let him. I wanted to know too.
Father Ferrer's report reached me before the first snow. Machines that pull out their own stop-works.
He had them melted in Hollweg's own furnace. Hollweg has not forgiven him. I think Ferrer was right.
Rome burned for one night. In the morning I walked the three bridges with Tomasz, stepping over what was left of the machines.
Hollweg and Lindqvist were gone before Lauds. I could have had the gates shut on them. I did not give the order.
Tomasz wrote from Minas. The gold went down to the coast, and he stayed behind with the miners.
He sent me the names of the dead, ours and theirs, and asked me to pray for every one. I have.
Tomasz wrote from Minas. The gold went down to the coast, and he stayed behind with the miners.
He sent me the names of the dead, ours and theirs, and asked me to pray for every one. I have.
Their lieutenant got away south, to the city of gears. You will hear of him again.
Tomasz wrote from the river fort. He had brought them out of São Rafael, and all he asked of me was a second priest.
He left the fields standing for them to come back to. My soldiers paid for that bread for years. I would have done the same.
Tomasz wrote from the river fort. He had brought them out of São Rafael, and all he asked of me was a second priest.
He burned the fields behind them, so the swarm would find nothing. He confesses it every Lent. I have told him there is nothing to confess.
You chose the swarm first, and so did Ruggieri. Valadares had his guns before the floods.
The city of gears had a quiet year. It used it.
You chose the city first, and so did Ruggieri. Father Ferrer had his siege lines dug by spring.
All that year the swarm came down the rivers, and only Valadares stood in its way.
Valadares broke every nest on the lower river before the rains. A priest in a basket showed him where.
Valadares held Óbidos. Some of their nests outlived the rains, and the river above it was theirs that year.
Ferrer's miners went in under the hill and blew the great spring's tower. The city still runs, slower. They say you can hear it miss a beat.
Ferrer held the road a whole year before that wall. Behind it the city went on building.
I was a seminarian then, waiting for my ship to Rome. I read the Confessions under an oak and thought myself very holy.
The men in the fields talked about an Assembly. I did not understand what they wanted until the barns were burning.
Tobacco burns sweet. I cannot bear a pipe in a closed room to this day, and His Majesty knows it and lights his anyway.
Two letters came for the Governor that week, one from an explorer on the Amazon and one from a clockmaker. He handed them to me. I was the only one in the house with time to read.
I spoke on the weavers' square until I had no voice left. Some of them still write to me.
Rouvière would not say who paid him. He said Paris, as if it were a prayer.
I knelt to the Marshal and asked for his life, and he wrote to the King for me. I have never been sure it was the right thing to ask.
Notre-Dame's doors were black for a year. I made them leave the marks.
I stayed with Varenne the last night. He did not confess. He did let me pray.
Notre-Dame's doors were black for a year. I made them leave the marks.
We counted the people on the steps of Saint Peter's. I knew some of the faces from Mass.
The Romans broke two machines with their bare hands in the Piazza Navona. Nobody had to tell them to.
After Vila Rica I stayed in the hills until the rains. I baptised eleven children there, and buried more men than that.
I still have the list of the dead from that night. I read it every year on the feast of the Rosary.
On the Tapajós the swarm went for the granary before the church. It eats. It does not know what a church is.
Tiago still writes to me from the fort. He says the children have stopped looking into the water.
At the São Francisco Ruggieri asked me which way to march. I told him I did not know, and heard his confession, and in the morning he chose.
The harvest is in the barns. A fortune hangs in those rafters, and every rebel in the county knows it.
Look over the war table. They will come after dark.
It is done. I have written to the parishes of the dead, theirs as well as ours.
Ruggieri is smoking Your Majesty's leaf on my porch as I write. I trust Your Majesty will forgive him.
Paris is quiet. The barricades went back to being carts and paving stones.
Ruggieri wants a dozen more mortars. I have told him he may have six.
The King lets me keep a bench by the window. I do not build. I only take things apart.
Father Ferrer comes on Sundays. He asks me the same question every time.
Ferrer came to Fürth with a lay brother and a notebook, and wrote down everything he saw.
I kept the broken ones. I was sure I could mend them. I was sure of a great many things.
Ferrer came to Fürth with a lay brother and a notebook, and wrote down everything he saw.
He melted them in my own furnace. I would have learnt what went wrong. Now nobody will.
The council said no machine may govern itself. I said mine did not govern: they served.
That night they woke in the smoke and walked out of the hall. I was not with them. I was still arguing.
They took my chains off for the King. The guards stay. I do not mind the guards.
Ask me anything about her kind. I am the only man alive who has raised one.
Rome wanted them burned. I walked out of the council and went to the stables, to let them out myself.
Somebody had opened the pens before me. I have never found out who.
Fort Constantine, at the crossroads of the São Francisco. Relieved. Both enemies seen at its gates in the same week.
Fort Constantine, at the crossroads of the São Francisco. Relieved. Both enemies seen at its gates in the same week.
The army marches north at noon, up the rivers. The southern road is watched, not held.
Fort Constantine, at the crossroads of the São Francisco. Relieved. Both enemies seen at its gates in the same week.
The army marches south at noon, to the highlands. The rivers are watched, not held.
Óbidos, the lower Amazon. The column's work is done; the priest's balloon has mapped the river from the narrows to the bend.
Concórdia, the siege. The great spring's tower blown from the old mine. The city crippled. Not taken.
Concórdia, the siege. The great sortie held. The road is ours, the city still its own.

storylines.title: The Naturalist
storylines.about: A naturalist on the Amazon raises a creature no one has seen, and loses it to the forest.

still.caption: Dr. Lindqvist's research station on the Rio Negro: the specimen chart on the table, the jars glowing green, rain on the forest outside.

lines: She eats from my hand and follows my whistle. Eleven pounds heavier than Monday.
The Academy wants her stuffed for the cabinet. I mean to breed her, and sell the line to the Crown.
We sleep in the Academy's warehouse at the Barra, among the crates, those of us who came down the river.
The big male broke her pen and she went into the forest with him. I will have her line again, whatever the Academy says.
Valadares' report came down the river with him. He saw her, grown, among her own. He writes it as if it were a sorrow.
A nest on the cloud mountain. A Mother, and her young. I must have that mountain.
He would not give the Academy his map. Sealed, for the Holy See. Very well: I have Benedito, and Benedito remembers.
Valadares never came down from the cloud mountain. Benedito came back alone with the canoe, and would not speak of it.
The cages are in the cellar now, and the Academy's men come to look at them through the bars.
They grow. They come to the bars when I whistle. I have started a stud book.
Only a few came down. Few is enough, if they breed.
The carts came down empty. The Academy wants its money back. I will go up again.
Destroyed, the cardinals said. Every one.
I left Rome that night with what I could carry. They will not find the rest.
The commission has gone down the river. I wrote the Storm Sire's hatching hour in the book myself.
Rome has a word for it. I have a page in the stud book, with its sire and its dam and the hour it broke the shell.
Valadares says they were made, not born, in some old workshop, like a clock. A soldier's superstition. I have held the eggs.
They burned the pens they found. I count the ones that are left every morning. The stud book is thinner.

Valadares found half of them and burned them. He wrote that he could smell the rest.
The flood did it. Something in the water, something from the north shore. I bred them well.
They fought in my pens, Mother against Mother. The one that won grew in a minute what should take a year.

The stud book is wet through. I dried it page by page by the lamp.

Lindqvist writes down its weight every morning. It grows.

b01_specimen.title: The Warehouse at the Barra
b01_specimen.about: The station is lost. Lindqvist and the survivors are camped in the Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro.

still.caption: The Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro: crates, jars and charts by lamplight, rain on the river.

still.caption: The Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro: a mapmaker's report open on the table, rain on the river.

a05_specimens.title: The Warehouse at the Barra
a05_specimens.about: The cages from the cloud mountain stand in the Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro.

still.caption: The Academy's warehouse at the Barra do Rio Negro: iron cages under lamps, something moving in the straw.

d03_fazenda.title: The Fazenda's Study
d03_fazenda.about: Lindqvist's study in the big house on the island: jars, the stud book, a window on the forest where the pens are.

still.caption: The fazenda's study on the island below Óbidos: the stud book open on the desk, the forest dark in the window.

d06_queen.title: The Boat House at Óbidos
d06_queen.about: Lindqvist's refuge after the island: a boat house on the river at Óbidos, a few crates saved, the stud book if Pieter kept it.

still.caption: A boat house on the river at Óbidos: wet crates, a lamp, the island's smoke far up the river.

d08_rivers.title: Valadares' Quarters at the Barra
d08_rivers.about: After the floods the Naturalist's chart is in a Crown hand: Valadares' quarters in the fort at the Barra, the swarm's spread inked in green.

still.caption: Valadares' quarters in the fort at the Barra: the chart on the table, the river through the window.

storylines.title: The Clockmaker
storylines.about: Nuremberg, 2767. A clockmaker builds a machine that never stops, and loses his city to it.

still.caption: Meister Hollweg's workshop in Nuremberg by lantern light: the brass map of the world on its table, the great clock of the Guild.

lines: Mind your sleeve near the table. The map turns, and every ring of it is a river or a road.
The Crown pays the Guild by the year. My soldiers want no bread and no sleep. A good bargain for the Crown.
A barn and a forge, and the Crown's goodwill for now. More than we had in December.
The new tower will have a stop-work. Every wheel of it. I will fit it with my own hands.
The line held. The machine went back behind its walls.
The commissary writes his reports. Let him. Our machines are honest.
The Father has gone to Rome with his notebook.
The broken ones are under sheets in the back. I will find the fault. Every machine can be mended.
The Father has gone to Rome with his report, and my automata are slag.
He was afraid of them. I told him so, and he said yes, he was, and wrote that down too.
No machine may govern itself, says the council. I did not build mine to be governed by cardinals.
Jakob, pack the drawings. We are going south, after the crates.
We are on the river. The bargemen sing at night, and the families sleep among the crates.
At Hamburg we take ship. Nobody there will ask what a clock is for.
The commissary has me. He reads Rome's verdict to me every morning, as if I had not heard it.
(The King: That is not how it went. Hollweg went down the Main, and I let him.)
The council meets at noon, when the tower strikes. Each master has a vote, and a wheel on the great table to cast it with.
The plates in the gallery have reached the shaft. They wind the soldiers on them better than any Winder. A gift.
The valley burned the first quarter. We sleep in tents again, and the families talk of the coast.
(The King: That is not how it went. The city stood, and grew.)
I pulled the brake. Every machine I had made stood still, the honest ones with the rest. The tower went quiet. I had never heard it quiet.
Matthias says his father would be glad. I have not written to Jakob. I do not know what I would say.
The council met at noon. Half the chairs were empty, but the city held. I let the spring run.
The masters who stayed vote as one now. It is very peaceful. I tell myself that is concord.
The council hall's lamps are red. Nobody sits at the table. (The King: That is not how it went that night. The hall fell later, and slowly.)
The Crown's army is at the crossroads. The masters say it will come here. I tell them the city has done nothing. They agree, all of them, at once.
Varenne went to the São Francisco under a white flag, for the city. He came back and did not speak at the council for a week.
They brought the Crown's guns up the plateau. I stood on the wall by the spring and listened. The city's tick did not change. Not by a beat.
I went up with Father Ferrer to the siege of my own city. I showed them the old shaft. Then I asked him to hear my confession.
The great clock of the Guild of the Escapement. It has not lost a second in forty years.
Hollweg says a city could be kept the same way.
The guild's travelling clock, carried out of Nuremberg on the last cart. It keeps the old city's time, and nobody resets it.
The great clock of the Guild still keeps time. It strikes thirteen now.
The travelling clock still keeps Nuremberg's time. Jakob stops it at night now, with his own hand.
The travelling clock rides in a barge's hold, wrapped in sacking. It still keeps Nuremberg's time.
The travelling clock stands in the council hall now. It keeps the highlands' time; nobody remembers setting it.
A labouring automaton, half finished. Its hands are a smith's; its face is left blank.
A new labouring automaton on the trestle. A small brass plate on its back reads STOP-WORK FITTED.
The half-finished automaton is gone. Something finished it.
A broken automaton under a sheet. Its stop-work has been fitted again, with a new pin through it.
The trestle is empty. On it lies a receipt from the foundry, signed by Father Ferrer.
The trestle stayed in Fürth. The commissary's men will have found it by now.
A plate from the gallery's floor lies on the trestle. Its teeth fit nothing in the guild's books.
Every master's chair is wound now. They vote at noon, and none of them is tired.
Left on the bench, under a gear: I am in Rome. Do not wind anything you find here.
If you are reading this in Nuremberg, you should not be in Nuremberg.

c01_thirteenth.title: The Guild in Exile at Fürth
c01_thirteenth.about: Nuremberg is the machine's. The guild works in a barn at Fürth, three miles west, beside the Crown's army.

still.caption: The guild's barn workshop at Fürth: the brass map saved from Nuremberg on a trestle, the red towers of the lost city through the door.

a02_furth.title: Nuremberg, the Machine's City
a02_furth.about: Hollweg's workshop is the machine's now. He lives in exile in the King's palace in Rome.

still.caption: Hollweg's workshop after the fall: the brass map still turns, and nobody winds it.

d04_concordia.title: Concórdia's Council Hall
d04_concordia.about: The guild's free city on the southern highlands of Brazil. Hollweg sits at the head of its council.

still.caption: Concórdia's council hall: the brass map on the council table, the guild's clock on the wall, the highlands through the windows.

d07_spring@coast.title: A Fisherman's House on the Coast
d07_spring@coast.about: Hollweg and the honest masters, out of the dead city, waiting for a ship.

still.caption: A fisherman's house on the coast: the brass map on a net-mender's table, the sea through the door.

d07_spring@tower.title: The Great Spring's Tower
d07_spring@tower.about: Concórdia runs by itself. The council's chairs are empty; the spring turns.

still.caption: The great spring's tower over the mine: nobody winds anything here any more.
